name: Modern liberalism in the United States
summary: American modern liberalism holds that freedom needs economic security as well as freedom from interference, so government should regulate markets and corporations, insure people against want and protect civil rights. It grew out of the Progressive reforms and Wilson's New Freedom, took its form in Roosevelt's New Deal and was given a philosophy by the new liberals.
scope: The mainstream American tradition that the Gale encyclopedia entry on liberalism describes as modern or twentieth-century liberalism: the turn, through the Progressive reforms and Wilson's New Freedom, to Roosevelt's New Deal in 1933, from opposing government in the economy to government as regulator and safety-net, and the new liberal philosophy that the Stanford Encyclopedia says is central to what is called liberalism in American politics. Its own texts here are Roosevelt's Second Bill of Rights message, his fireside chats and speeches of 1934-1941 (the Gale entry names him as the one who introduced it) and Wilson's The New Freedom. It excludes classical liberalism, American libertarianism, the Democratic Party's platforms (a party is not the ideology) and Rawls's liberal egalitarianism as such.

ban-cartels.rationale: The encyclopedia says the federal government under Wilson and the Progressives moved to 'break up monopolies' (the Clayton Act), Wilson's New Freedom attacks the trusts, and Roosevelt pledged in 1936 to 'end monopoly in business'.

central-planning.rationale: Roosevelt (1934) said the New Deal had avoided 'the theory that business should and must be taken over into an all-embracing Government', preferring regulation 'only to meet concrete needs'.

conscription.rationale: Roosevelt's 1944 message defends selective service for the armed forces as resting 'on the obligation of each citizen to serve his Nation' and asks for a national service law.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Roosevelt (1938) set the liberal's democratic processes against 'Fascism or Communism' and called the 'wild man who, in effect, leans in the direction of Communism' just as dangerous as Fascism.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Roosevelt's 1944 message promises security 'for all regardless of station, race, or creed', and the Stanford Encyclopedia gives liberal tradition 'equality before the law' and an equal right to basic liberty.

gradual-change.rationale: Roosevelt (1934) described the American practice of government as 'a practice of taking action step by step, of regulating only to meet concrete needs', while rejecting a 'moratorium on reform' (1938).

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Roosevelt (1941) listed among the basic expectations of the people 'the enjoyment of the fruits of scientific progress in a wider and constantly rising standard of living'.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: New liberals lost faith in the unregulated market and put faith in government 'as a means of supervising economic life'; the encyclopedia describes modern liberalism as protecting the national economy against the unregulated tendency towards instability.

more-religion-public.rationale: Roosevelt (1936) said 'democracy cannot live without that true religion which gives a nation a sense of justice and of moral purpose'; he did not describe a role for religion in law or government.

nation-first.rationale: Roosevelt (1941) sought 'the cooperation of free countries, working together in a friendly, civilized society', and (1937) 'the cooperative search for peace by all the nations which want peace'.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The encyclopedia says modern liberalism turned from opposing government in the economy to the roles of 'regulator and safety-net', and Roosevelt asked Congress to implement economic rights, which no government limited to protecting people from violence could do.

one-party-rule.rationale: Roosevelt (1938) defined the liberal as believing in 'progressive principles of democratic, representative government' and said problems are solved 'through democratic processes instead of Fascism or Communism'.

positive-liberty.rationale: Roosevelt held that 'true individual freedom cannot exist without economic security and independence', and the Stanford Encyclopedia sets out the new liberal view of positive liberty as what matters for the working class.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Roosevelt's 1944 message asks Congress for a food law 'to place a ceiling on the prices a consumer will have to pay for the food he buys', for necessities only, in time of war.

property-fundamental.rationale: The Stanford Encyclopedia says new liberals reject property as 'the guardian of every other right', holding that property rights 'foster an unjust inequality of power', a theme it calls central to American liberalism.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Roosevelt in 1937 called for 'reasonable minimum wages and maximum hours' and in 1944 listed 'the right to earn enough to provide adequate food and clothing and recreation'.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Wilson's New Freedom calls dealings of great corporations 'a matter of public regulation', and Roosevelt (1934) favoured 'regulating only to meet concrete needs' rather than leaving business alone or taking it into government; the encyclopedia gives modern liberalism the roles of 'regulator and safety-net'.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The Stanford Encyclopedia presents the principle that the king 'is bound by the rule of law' and that political authority must be justified as the root of constitutional liberalism.

state-harmful.rationale: Modern liberalism gives the government the roles of regulator and safety-net (encyclopedia), and Roosevelt asked Congress to implement the economic bill of rights; abolishing the state contradicts both.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Wilson's New Freedom attacks 'the extravagant tariff' as governmental favoritism, the encyclopedia lists lowering tariffs among the Progressive reforms, and Roosevelt (1937) called for 'the reduction of trade barriers'.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Roosevelt held in 1941 that 'the principle of tax payments in accordance with ability to pay should be constantly before our eyes to guide our legislation'.

taxation-theft.rationale: Roosevelt's 1944 message asks Congress for 'a realistic tax law' to 'share equitably the burdens of taxation' and in 1941 for tax payments by ability to pay, treating taxation as a legitimate public power.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Roosevelt's fourth freedom (1941) was a world-wide reduction of armaments 'to such a point ... that no nation will be in a position to commit an act of physical aggression against any neighbor'.

total-state.rationale: Roosevelt (1934) rejected 'the theory that business should and must be taken over into an all-embracing Government', and (1938) set liberal democratic processes against Fascism and Communism.

unions-good.rationale: Roosevelt said 'we have recognized the right of labor to free organization, to collective bargaining' and pledged in 1936 to 'support collective bargaining'.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Roosevelt's 1944 Second Bill of Rights lists 'the right to adequate medical care and the opportunity to achieve and enjoy good health' and asks Congress to implement it; in 1941 he asked to 'widen the opportunities for adequate medical care'.

notes: This pass (2026-11-12) rebuilt the audit to rules 7. The earlier answers rested mostly on the Democratic Party's 2024 platform (a party's platform is a coatrack for an ideology) and on Wikipedia, or on the idea that liberals 'would' reject something; those were nulled with their old versions kept in reviewHistory. Defining sources read: Stanford Encyclopedia (Liberalism), the Gale encyclopedia entry, Roosevelt's 1944 message, 1941 Four Freedoms message, 1934-1938 fireside chats and 1936 Madison Square Garden speech, Wilson 1913. Dewey's Liberalism and Social Action and the Stanford entry on his politics were read but not cited: no defining source ties him to this ideology alone (he is also a defining author of pragmatism). Themes searched in them: economy, regulation, unions, taxes, tariffs, property, the state, equality, democracy, violence versus reform, church and state, foreign affairs, civil liberties, ecology. Gender and family, minority and territorial questions, and nationalism have no position in the open texts of Roosevelt, Wilson or the encyclopedias (searched for women, family, minorities, race, immigration, language, secession, patriotism). Most other themes (the criminal law, drugs, guns, migration, abortion, same-sex marriage, the environment, foreign policy, religion, family) have no position in these sources, so they stay null; failing the uncertainty rule is the honest result. Not found: Rawls's own books and the Galbraith and Schlesinger texts were not available as open copies in this pass.
